problem: The endpoint descriptions for exclusive and inclusive classes are swapped. Exclusive classes DO share an endpoint (10–20 and 20–30 both contain the written value 20); inclusive classes do NOT (10–19 and 20–29 leave a gap between 19 and 20). As written, the two sentences contradict the very examples given next to them, and contradict the rest of the chapter (the 0.5 conversion, exam trap 2).
fix: Exclusive classes have no gap: the upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next, as in 10–20 and 20–30, and a value of 20 belongs to 20–30. Inclusive classes have a gap: 10–19 and 20–29, where the upper limit 19 and the next lower limit 20 are different written values.

problem: Wrong consequence. Drawing inclusive classes 10–19 and 20–29 without adjusting leaves a gap of 1 unit between the bars; it does not make the bars overlap. 'Overlap' is the opposite of what happens, and it also contradicts the standard reason for adjusting (bars must touch).
fix: Inclusive classes 10–19 and 20–29 need boundaries 9.5–19.5 and 19.5–29.5; if you forget the 0.5 adjustment, the histogram bars are separated by a 1-unit gap instead of touching.

problem: Same error as the trap, plus the phrase 'overlap at the gap' is self-contradictory. With written limits 10–19 and 20–29 the bars are 9 units wide if plotted literally, so a gap appears; nothing overlaps.
fix: The bars fail to touch. Plotted at the written limits the first bar ends at 19 and the next starts at 20, leaving a gap of 1 unit, and the bar widths are 9 instead of 10. Convert to boundaries 9.5–19.5 and 19.5–29.5 so the bars touch exactly and each has width 10.

problem: Setting height = frequency is correct only when all class widths are equal. If the classes have different widths, a frequency-height histogram misrepresents the data.
fix: Histogram: bars touch, one per class, width = class width. With equal widths the height is the frequency f; with unequal widths the height is the frequency density f / (class width).

problem: 'It also draws the first picture, the histogram or ogive' says the frequency table draws the picture, which a student may read literally. The table is drawn from, not drawing.
fix: The frequency table also gives the first picture, the histogram or the ogive, because both are drawn straight from its counts.
